docs.title: ADR-001: Editable multiline chat input
docs.text:
Status: Accepted; implemented.

Date: 2026-11-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Chat users need to compose, paste and edit messages spanning several lines, then submit the complete buffer as one message. Enter should submit rather than insert a newline.

PICLE already uses a persistent prompt_toolkit.PromptSession for interactive input. Rich renders responses and remains optional. The installed prompt-toolkit 3.0.52 supports multiline editing and a frame around the input. Reusing this backend avoids introducing a second terminal input system.

Two existing behaviors need explicit handling: _run_chat_shell() strips the entire message, and _PicleHistory persists one physical line per entry. Multiline messages should retain indentation and should not reload as several independent shell history entries.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Use a fixed-height multiline editor with top and bottom separator lines and vertical scrolling for every chat session. Chat models continue to enable chat through the existing setting:

class PicleConfig:
    chat_shell = True

Do not add a chat_multiline setting or a separate single-line chat mode. Use prompt-toolkit's TextArea inside a small non-full-screen application layout without side borders. Keep the visible editor height bounded while allowing the message to grow beyond it; scroll with the cursor and show a vertical scrollbar. Omit the keyboard-controls hint to save terminal space. Rich continues to render responses outside the active editor.

Action Behavior Enter Submit the complete buffer as one message. Alt+Enter / Escape, then Enter Insert a newline by default. Arrow keys Move within the editable buffer, scrolling when needed. Bracketed multiline paste Insert all pasted text without submitting it.

If a completion is active, Enter accepts it before submitting the message, preserving the existing completion interaction. Configure the app-wide newline sequence using chat_newline_keys in the root model's PicleConfig. Its default is the user-facing name "alt+enter", translated internally to ("escape", "enter"). A key name such as "c-j" replaces the default with Ctrl+J; a terminal mapping can then send that sequence for Shift+Enter. The chat documentation provides the VS Code mapping.

Preserve the original message buffer for the handler. Ignore whitespace-only input. Check for line breaks in the original buffer before stripping whitespace for slash-command parsing. Only single-line input beginning with / is dispatched as a command; a multiline buffer remains one message even when a line begins with /. This also applies to a buffer with a trailing newline.

Keep all chat input in separate in-memory history for the app instance. Do not mix chat messages with shell commands or persist them to the shell's history file. Preserve the existing shell history file format.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Rich prompts: useful for formatted prompts, but do not provide the editable multiline buffer required here. Retain Rich for response output.
  • Default prompt-toolkit multiline bindings: Enter inserts a newline and Alt+Enter submits. Use Enter to submit and an app-configurable newline sequence, defaulting to Alt+Enter.
  • Expanding framed prompt: needs less layout work but grows with the message. Select a fixed-height text area to keep the visible editor bounded.
  • Opt-in multiline setting: preserves the old chat editor but adds a second input mode to configure and maintain. Use multiline input for all chat.
  • New persistent history format: could retain complete multiline entries across runs, but adds migration and compatibility work beyond this feature.

docs.title: Implementation outline
docs.text:
1. Keep the editor and chat loop in ChatShell in picle/chat.py. App._run_chat_shell() delegates to the single persistent ChatShell.run() application. Normal shell input remains in App._read_interactive_input(). Use a prompt-toolkit TextArea, top and bottom separator lines, scrollbar in a non-full-screen layout. Reuse existing completion adapter and a separate in-memory chat history. Keep the normal shell's persistent PromptSession and load-terminal input path unchanged.
  2. Add submit and newline bindings local to the chat editor, including active completion handling. Ensure the editor releases terminal control on normal completion and exceptions. Avoid using self.is_chat alone to select the reader, since slash commands can also request ordinary field input.
  3. Use ChatShell.run() to preserve multiline message whitespace and apply the single-line slash-command rule. Keep lifecycle hooks, response outputters and existing idle Ctrl+C and EOF behavior.
  4. Use a separate InMemoryHistory for chat input, retaining it across chat sessions in the same app instance. Keep ordinary shell input and load-terminal collection unchanged.
  5. Document the editor, controls, command routing and history limitation in the chat interface page, and add a changelog entry when implemented.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
No new dependency or full-screen application is needed. Every existing chat model receives the new editor automatically. Ordinary shell input remains unchanged.

Custom bindings and editor layout must be tested together with completion and paste handling. Multiline messages will not be available in history after restarting PICLE. Persistent multiline history can be considered separately.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• Use real prompt-toolkit pipe input with DummyOutput to verify submission, newline insertion, cross-line edits, bracketed paste and completion. Assert that ordinary shell reads retain their original settings afterward.
  • Use public App.onecmd() tests to verify one handler call per multiline buffer, preserved whitespace, slash-command routing and hooks running once per session. Exercise history save and reload to ensure multiline entries cannot split into shell commands.
  • Manually verify Windows VS Code terminal behavior: editing previous lines, wrapping, fixed viewport height, scrolling through long messages, terminal resizing, paste, completion, submission and return to the shell.
  • Run poetry run pytest -q, Black checks on changed Python files, and a strict MkDocs build targeting a temporary directory.

docs.title: Implementation detail
docs.text: The viewport defaults to five text rows. The chat model's PicleConfig.chat_input_height configures its height, excluding separator lines. Reduce it to fit the available terminal height, with a minimum of one row.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Prompt-toolkit prompts, multiline input and frames
  • Prompt-toolkit key bindings and terminal constraints
  • Prompt-toolkit application layouts and widgets
  • Rich prompts

docs.title: Persistent layout extension
docs.text:
Keep one prompt-toolkit application alive during each chat session. Permanent output goes to terminal scrollback; status, approval and input sections share one renderer below it. Handlers run in a worker thread. Input remains editable while busy, but submission and Ctrl+C/Ctrl+D termination are disabled until the operation finishes. No queued or overlapping operations are allowed.

Expose ChatSession.write(text), set_status(text="", spinner=False), and approve(prompt) -> bool. Inject the session only into the active handler when it explicitly names chat; hooks receive command arguments only. Handler updates are scheduled onto an ordered async UI queue. Additional callback threads and concurrent approval requests are outside the supported scope. The status row uses prompt-toolkit refreshes for animation. Approvals focus an Allow/Deny section and block the worker, not the UI. Teardown denies pending approvals and clears the chat flag. Hooks do not write session progress, so there is no post-UI output flush. Do not snapshot or restore shell state: /exit uses normal shell exit handling; EOF, errors and handler termination may leave the slash-command model mounted. Nested chats and shell navigation through slash commands are unsupported; custom slash commands remain available.

Streaming responses are removed. Handlers return complete answers, rendered once using the existing outputter path. Arbitrary print/log capture, Rich Live, cooperative cancellation and transcript navigation remain outside this scope.

ChatSession.set_footer(text="") replaces an optional row below the bottom separator. It persists between messages and handler errors until replaced or cleared, and resets when the session ends. Long content is clipped without wrapping; a visible footer reduces the editor's available height by one row. It uses the existing event queue and requires no additional setting.

write() accepts plain strings. Footers accept strings and prompt-toolkit formatted text; status accepts plain strings. Layout widgets and Rich objects are outside the session interface.

docs.title: ADR-002: SSH server support
docs.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: 2026-09-05
  • Scope: Architecture proposal; implementation pending

docs.title: Context
docs.text: PICLE needs a design for optional remote interactive sessions over SSH on Windows and Linux. The transport must bridge asynchronous SSH streams and PICLE's synchronous command execution while isolating each session's state, output and history. Host-account authentication and command authorization must remain separate from the OS identity under which commands execute.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Use AsyncSSH as an optional embedded transport with these authentication methods:

  • Linux host usernames and passwords through a dedicated PAM service.
  • Windows local or domain usernames and passwords through LogonUser.
  • SSH public keys as an additional method.

Authorize authenticated users against canonical PICLE command paths. Support user and group policies with allow and deny rules. deny always overrides allow; the default policy is allow * for backward compatibility and simple deployments.

Authentication does not change process identity. Embedded sessions run as the PICLE server account. Deployments which require commands to run as the authenticated host user should use system OpenSSH to launch a separate PICLE process.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
AsyncSSH can serve an interactive PICLE session on Windows and Linux. It supports server-side shell sessions, public-key and password authentication, terminal metadata, and line editing. It also requires Python 3.10+, matching PICLE. See the AsyncSSH documentation and package metadata.

The proposed host-password design has a critical identity problem: authenticating a host user does not make an in-process PICLE session run as that user. Commands still run as the account hosting the PICLE server.

This is unsafe with PICLE's current shell command, which executes arbitrary OS commands. If the server runs as root, SYSTEM, an administrator, or another privileged account, every accepted user may gain that account's privileges.

Host authentication is also platform-specific:

  • Linux requires a dedicated PAM service and account-policy handling, not only a call to pam_authenticate(). See the Linux-PAM interface.
  • Windows LogonUser validates credentials and returns a token. Impersonation or creating a process under that token is a separate operation with additional privilege and lifecycle requirements. See LogonUser.

PAM and LogonUser authentication are feasible, but must be isolated behind platform-specific providers and run away from the asyncio event loop. System OpenSSH remains the better mode when OS-user process identity is required.

docs.title: Feasibility
docs.text: Area Rating Main issue AsyncSSH transport High Mature server API and compatible Python version. Basic remote PICLE session Medium-high Requires an adapter between async SSH streams and PICLE's synchronous loop. Local terminal feature parity Medium prompt_toolkit, completion, inline help, interrupts, and terminal control need remote-specific handling. Concurrent sessions Medium Output, history, model state, and blocking commands must be isolated. Linux host authentication Medium Requires PAM service and account/session policy. Windows host authentication Medium Requires LogonUser, token handling, and platform-specific process creation. In-process host-user isolation Low Authentication does not change the server process identity. Public Internet exposure Low initially Requires rate limits, auditing, timeouts, secure defaults, and security testing.

docs.title: Current PICLE constraints
docs.text:
• App.start() and cmdloop() are synchronous and blocking.
  • AsyncSSH readers are asynchronous; PICLE expects file-like readline() and write() methods.
  • prompt_toolkit expects a local terminal.
  • Rich uses a module-global console instead of App.stdout, which can mix or misroute output.
  • All sessions default to the same picle_history.txt file.
  • cls clears the server terminal instead of the SSH client.
  • shell runs commands as the server process account.
  • Application models may contain mutable state that is unsafe to share between sessions.

Each SSH channel therefore needs a new App and root-model instance, isolated output, and isolated or disabled history.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Option Benefits Problems Decision Embedded AsyncSSH with PAM or LogonUser Reuses host accounts without requiring system SSH. Platform-specific; sessions still run as the shared server account. Selected embedded mode. Embedded AsyncSSH with public keys Portable and avoids reusable passwords. Requires key provisioning; sessions still use the server account. Supported alternative. System OpenSSH launches PICLE Real host identity, process isolation, mature authentication and auditing. Requires administrator setup and platform-specific documentation. Preferred host-identity mode. Privileged broker launching per-user workers Combines embedded SSH with OS-user isolation. Complex privileged service which duplicates much of sshd. Defer.

OpenSSH can restrict users to PICLE through a forced command or subsystem. Forwarding must be disabled separately. See the OpenSSH server configuration manual and Windows OpenSSH configuration.

docs.title: Proposed architecture
docs.text:
Embedded mode

SSH client
  -> AsyncSSH listener
  -> platform authenticator (PAM, LogonUser, or public key)
  -> command-tree authorizer
  -> new PICLE session
  -> remote terminal adapter

Host-identity mode

SSH client
  -> system OpenSSH
  -> restricted PICLE launcher
  -> new PICLE process running as the host user

Keep SSH outside App. Provide a separate optional API such as:

picle.ssh.serve(root_factory, config)

Main components:

  • SSHServerConfig: listener, host keys, authentication methods, authorization policy, timeouts, limits, and audit settings.
  • Authenticator: validates credentials and returns a normalized principal with username and host groups.
  • Authorizer: evaluates the principal against canonical command paths.
  • SessionFactory: creates a new root model and App for each channel.
  • RemoteTerminal: handles input, output, newlines, interrupts, resize events, and disconnects.
  • ServerHandle: provides explicit start, stop, and wait operations.

Prefer an asynchronous PICLE session driver which awaits complete lines and calls the existing parser and dispatcher. A bounded worker-thread bridge is acceptable for a prototype but adds cancellation, shutdown, and backpressure complexity.

Do not promise full prompt_toolkit parity in the first release. Initial support should cover line editing, execution, help commands, clean disconnects, and predictable terminal output.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Use a dedicated PAM service, for example picle-ssh. Authentication must include the configured PAM authentication and account checks so locked, expired, or otherwise ineligible accounts are rejected. End every PAM transaction and do not retain the password.

PAM calls may block and must run in a bounded worker executor. Treat PAM errors as authentication failures externally while retaining safe diagnostic detail in server logs.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Use LogonUser with a documented logon type and provider. Support explicit local and domain username formats. Close every returned token handle after authentication.

The token proves the credentials were accepted; it does not make the in-process PICLE session execute as that user. Do not use thread impersonation in the shared server process. Per-user execution requires a separate process or system OpenSSH.

docs.title: Common requirements
docs.text:
• Password authentication must be explicitly enabled in server configuration.
  • Never place passwords in command-line arguments, configuration files, logs, audit events, or session objects.
  • Apply authentication timeouts and rate limits by source and username.
  • Return indistinguishable failures for unknown users and incorrect passwords.
  • Run PAM, LogonUser, and other blocking identity-provider calls outside the event loop.
  • Perform command authorization after authentication succeeds.

docs.title: Command-tree authorization
docs.text:
Authorization rules operate on canonical PICLE model and command paths, not the raw input string. Aliases and serialization aliases must resolve to the same canonical path before evaluation.

Pattern syntax:

  • * matches every command.
  • show matches the show node itself.
  • show * matches every command below show.
  • show version matches only that command path.

Policy example:

default: allow
groups:
  operators:
    allow:
      - "show *"
    deny:
      - "show secrets"
users:
  alice:
    deny:
      - "shell"

Evaluation order:

  1. Collect rules for the authenticated user and their host groups.
  2. Resolve the entered command to its canonical path.
  3. If any deny rule matches, deny the command.
  4. Otherwise, if any allow rule matches, allow it.
  5. Otherwise, use default, which is allow unless configured differently.

An administrator can build a strict allow-list by setting default: deny and adding rules such as allow: ["show *"]. Because explicit deny has priority, an allow rule cannot override a matching deny rule.

Authorization must be applied consistently to:

  • Command execution, immediately before dispatch.
  • Help, command-tree output, discovery, and completion so denied paths are not advertised. A model node remains visible when it contains at least one visible command.
  • Dynamically mounted models and commands.
  • Built-in commands such as shell, history, and navigation commands.

The execution check is authoritative. Hiding a command from help or completion is not a security control.

The default allow * policy includes built-in commands such as shell. This preserves existing PICLE behavior but means every authenticated user can execute commands with the server account's privileges unless an administrator adds an explicit deny rule. Production examples should deny shell unless it is required.

docs.title: Consequences and required defaults
docs.text:
• Bind to loopback unless external listening is explicitly configured.
  • Require a persistent host key; fail closed if it is missing or insecure.
  • Support PAM on Linux, LogonUser on Windows, and SSH public keys.
  • Require password authentication to be explicitly enabled.
  • Separate authentication from authorization.
  • Default command authorization to allow *; allow deployments to select default: deny.
  • Make explicit deny rules override every allow rule.
  • Run under a dedicated unprivileged service account.
  • Accept one interactive shell channel per connection by default.
  • Reject SSH exec, subsystems, SFTP/SCP, forwarding, and extra channels.
  • Set authentication, idle, connection, session, and output limits.
  • Do not accept client environment variables by default.
  • Do not log passwords, private keys, or command results.
  • Disable remote persistent history by default. If enabled, isolate it by principal.
  • Document that allow * includes shell and other high-risk commands; provide explicit deny examples for production deployments.
  • Route all output, including Rich output, through the session writer.
  • Pin to a maintained AsyncSSH release. Version 2.22.0 must be excluded because of CVE-2026-45309, fixed in 2.23.0.

docs.title: Delivery sequence
docs.text:
1. Separate terminal input/output from command parsing and dispatch.
  2. Make output and history session-specific.
  3. Test concurrent session isolation.
  4. Add command-path authorization and filter execution, help, discovery, and completion.
  5. Add optional AsyncSSH transport and public-key authentication.
  6. Add PAM and LogonUser providers with rate limits and audit events.
  7. Test Windows and Linux clients, PTY behavior, disconnects, slow clients, and blocking commands.
  8. Document system OpenSSH deployment for per-user process identity.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• Missing or unavailable authentication providers fail closed.
  • PAM and LogonUser enforce host account status and do not block unrelated sessions.
  • Host identity is stable across restarts.
  • Only the interactive PICLE shell is exposed.
  • Concurrent clients cannot share output, history, shell state, or application state unintentionally.
  • Blocking commands do not stall authentication or unrelated sessions.
  • Slow clients cannot cause unbounded memory growth.
  • Disconnects, cancellation, exceptions, and shutdown release all resources.
  • The server runs without root or administrator privileges.
  • Documentation states which OS account executes commands.
  • Authorization uses canonical paths, supports * and subtree patterns, and gives deny rules priority.
  • Authorization is enforced during execution and reflected in help, discovery, and completion.
  • The default policy is allow *, and default: deny produces a strict allow-list.
  • Authentication failure, authorization denial, and session lifecycle events are auditable without logging secrets.

docs.title: Chat Interface
docs.text: Use chat mode to exchange messages with an agent and run commands without leaving the conversation. The message editor stays visible while a response is being prepared. Progress, status and approval requests appear above it.

docs.title: Basic example
docs.text:
Set chat_shell = True on the chat model and define run() to handle each submitted message:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from picle import App


class AgentModel(BaseModel):
    @staticmethod
    def run(message, **kwargs):
        return f"I received: {message}"

    class PicleConfig:
        chat_shell = True
        chat_prompt = "You> "
        chat_response_prefix = "AI> "


class Root(BaseModel):
    agent: AgentModel = Field(None, description="Chat with the agent")


App(Root).start()

Enter agent at the shell prompt to start chatting. Type /exit on a single line to return to the parent shell.

For a working example, run this command from the repository root:

poetry run python -m test.example_chat_app

Then enter chat session_id demo user alice. Try work for progress updates, fail for an example error, approve for an approval request, or rich for styled text and a table (requires Rich).

docs.title: Writing messages
docs.text:
Key Action Enter Send the message. If a completion is selected, accept it first. Alt+Enter Insert a newline by default. Tab Complete a slash command. Arrow keys Move within the message; Up/Down also recall earlier chat input.

Paste or type several lines, edit them, then press Enter to send the complete message. Spaces, tabs and line breaks are kept as entered. Pressing Enter on empty or whitespace-only input does nothing.

The editor shows five text rows by default, wraps long lines and scrolls as you move through longer messages. Set chat_input_height to change its height; it shrinks to fit smaller terminals.

Use the terminal's scroll controls to review earlier messages and responses. Chat input history is separate from shell command history and is available across chat sessions until the app closes. Chat input is not saved to disk.

While a response is being prepared, you can compose the next message, but must wait for the current operation to finish before sending it. Ctrl+C and Ctrl+D do not cancel a running operation or close a busy chat.

docs.title: PicleConfig options
docs.text:
Set these options on the chat model, except chat_newline_keys, which belongs on the root model and applies to all chat sessions.

Option Default Description chat_shell False Enable chat mode for this model. chat_prompt "> " Prefix shown with submitted messages. chat_input_height 5 Visible text rows, excluding separator lines. Uses at least one row and shrinks to fit the terminal. chat_newline_keys "alt+enter" Newline shortcut for all chats. Accepts "alt+enter", a key name such as "c-j" for Ctrl+J, or a tuple of key names for a sequence. chat_response_style None Response style such as "green" or "bold cyan". Requires Rich and use_rich = True. chat_response_prefix "" Prefix shown before responses, such as "AI> ". chat_commands_model None Model defining custom slash commands.

For example, to show eight input rows and green responses:

class PicleConfig:
    chat_shell = True
    chat_input_height = 8
    chat_response_prefix = "AI> "
    chat_response_style = "green"

docs.title: Changing the newline shortcut
docs.text:
Configure chat_newline_keys on the root model:

class Root(BaseModel):
    agent: AgentModel = None

    class PicleConfig:
        chat_newline_keys = "c-j"  # Ctrl+J; default is "alt+enter"

The new shortcut replaces Alt+Enter. To use Shift+Enter, configure "c-j" as above and map Shift+Enter to a line feed in your terminal. In VS Code, add this entry to your user keybindings.json:

{
    "key": "shift+enter",
    "command": "workbench.action.terminal.sendSequence",
    "args": {"text": "\u000a"},
    "when": "terminalFocus"
}

docs.title: Slash commands
docs.text:
A single-line message beginning with / runs a command instead of sending a message to the agent. Define custom commands with chat_commands_model:

from typing import Any


class ChatCommands(BaseModel):
    usage: Any = Field(None, json_schema_extra={"function": "show_usage"})

    @staticmethod
    def show_usage():
        return "1234 tokens used"


class AgentModel(BaseModel):
    @staticmethod
    def run(message, **kwargs):
        return f"Echo: {message}"

    class PicleConfig:
        chat_shell = True
        chat_commands_model = ChatCommands

In this example, /usage displays the custom usage report. It is not a built-in command. Type /exit to leave chat. Commands that ask for additional input may temporarily hide the message editor until you finish answering.

A message containing any line break is always sent to the agent, even if it starts with / or has only a trailing newline. Nested chats and shell navigation from slash commands are not supported.

docs.title: Progress, status and approvals
docs.text:
Add a named chat parameter to run() to show progress or ask for approval:

class AgentModel(BaseModel):
    @staticmethod
    def run(message, chat, **kwargs):
        chat.set_footer("Model: local | Session: demo")
        chat.set_status("Thinking", spinner=True, elapsed=True)
        chat.write("Checking the request")
        if not chat.approve("Allow this action?"):
            return "Action denied"
        chat.write("Action allowed")
        return f"Completed: {message}"

    class PicleConfig:
        chat_shell = True
Method Use chat.write(text) Add a progress message above the editor. Accepts plain strings or Rich renderables. Embedded newlines are preserved; a final newline is optional. chat.set_status(text="", spinner=False, elapsed=False) Replace the temporary status line. Use spinner=True for activity and elapsed=True for elapsed minutes and seconds. Replacing the status resets the timer. Call with no text to clear it; status also clears when the operation finishes. chat.set_footer(text="") Replace the single-line footer below the editor. Accepts plain strings or prompt-toolkit formatted text. It stays between messages, including after an error. Call with no text to hide it. Long text is clipped to the available width. chat.approve(prompt) Ask the user to press Y to Allow or N to Deny. Returns True or False.

Use the following examples inside run(message, chat, **kwargs). Plain strings are displayed as written. For styled output, use Rich objects with write() or prompt-toolkit formatted text with set_footer().

WriteStatusFooter

Add progress messages above the editor. Each call adds a new entry; embedded newlines are preserved.

Plain text

chat.write("Checking the request")
chat.write("Step 1 complete\nStarting step 2")

Styled text with Rich

With Rich installed and use_rich = True, you can also write styled text, tables and panels:

from rich.text import Text
from rich.table import Table

chat.write(Text("Request accepted", style="bold green"))

table = Table("Step", "Result")
table.add_row("Check request", "Passed")
chat.write(table)

Without Rich output enabled, objects are shown as their plain string representation. Return the final answer normally instead of also writing it here.

Show a temporary message while work is in progress:

chat.set_status("Checking the request")

Show cycling dots after the text, followed by elapsed time, such as Thinking... 00:12:

chat.set_status("Thinking", spinner=True, elapsed=True)
# Perform your operation here.

Replace or clear the status:

chat.set_status("Finishing...")  # replaces the previous status
chat.set_status()               # clears it

Replacing the status resets its timer. Status clears automatically when the operation finishes. Status text accepts plain strings.

Show session information below the editor. Setting a footer replaces its previous content; it stays between messages until replaced or cleared.

Plain text

chat.set_footer("Model: local | Session: demo")

Prompt-toolkit formatted text

from prompt_toolkit.formatted_text import HTML

chat.set_footer(HTML("<b>Model:</b> local | <ansigreen>Connected</ansigreen>"))

Hide the footer:

chat.set_footer()

The footer occupies one row; long content is clipped. It resets when the chat session ends.

For more footer styles, you can also use prompt-toolkit ANSI, FormattedText, styled text fragments, or a function that returns formatted text. The footer stays one row high regardless of the content.

docs.title: Supported content types
docs.text:
Method Plain strings Prompt-toolkit formatted text Rich objects chat.write() Yes Not supported Yes, when Rich is installed and use_rich = True; otherwise shown as a string chat.set_footer() Yes Yes: HTML, ANSI, FormattedText, styled fragments and callables Not supported, including Rich Text chat.set_status() Yes Not supported Not supported, including Rich Text and Rich spinners

For a styled footer, use prompt-toolkit HTML or FormattedText. For status animation and timing, use the spinner=True and elapsed=True arguments. Rich renderables such as Text, Panel and Table can be passed to write(), but not to status or footer. Console, Live and prompt-toolkit layout widgets are not supported.

Strings are always plain text: "[green]Ready[/green]" and "<b>Ready</b>" are displayed literally rather than interpreted as markup.

docs.title: Asking for approval
docs.text:
Call chat.approve("Allow this action?") before an action that needs the user's permission. Pressing Y returns True; pressing N returns False. Your handler waits for that choice before continuing.

While the request is visible, the keyboard answers it. After the choice, you can edit messages again. Ask for one approval at a time. If chat closes unexpectedly, the request is denied.

Use these methods only inside run(). Add chat to its parameter list; **kwargs alone does not receive it. Hooks and background callbacks cannot use the session methods. Keep the name chat for this parameter rather than using it for a command argument.

Return the final answer normally; do not also send it with chat.write(). Response prefixes, styles and outputters continue to apply. Return a complete answer rather than a generator or iterator. Use chat.write() for progress instead of print(), terminal logs or a separate live display.

docs.title: Session hooks
docs.text:
Use chat_on_enter() to initialize context before the first message and chat_on_exit() to clean it up when chat ends. Define them on the chat model, not inside PicleConfig:

context = {}


class AgentModel(BaseModel):
    topic: str = "general"

    @staticmethod
    def chat_on_enter(**kwargs):
        context["topic"] = kwargs["topic"]

    @staticmethod
    def chat_on_exit(**kwargs):
        context.clear()

    @staticmethod
    def run(message, **kwargs):
        return f"{context['topic']}: {message}"

    class PicleConfig:
        chat_shell = True

The entry hook runs once before the first message, and the exit hook runs once when the session ends. You can define either hook or both. Both receive command arguments and defaults, with explicit arguments taking precedence. They do not receive the chat object, and their return values are ignored.

If command validation fails, neither hook runs. If entry fails, chat does not open and exit is not called; clean up any partially initialized context in the entry hook. Exit errors are reported and can prevent a requested app termination from taking effect.

docs.title: Ending a session
docs.text:
• /exit leaves chat and returns to the parent shell.
  • Ctrl+D on an empty editor ends chat while idle.
  • Ctrl+C while idle ends chat and terminates the app.
  • Returning None from run() ends chat.
  • Returning True from run() ends chat and terminates the app.

After Ctrl+D or a handler ending chat, a configured slash-command shell may remain active. Use exit to return to its parent shell.

Handler errors are displayed so the user can try another message. The exit hook runs when the session ends, including after an error that closes chat.

docs.title: Command Discovery
docs.text: PICLE's discovery flow is model-driven. The same field metadata powers inline help, the help command, tab completion, and the built-in man commands.

docs.title: Example Model
docs.text:
from enum import Enum
from typing import List, Union
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, StrictStr


class ConnectionPlugin(str, Enum):
    netmiko = "netmiko"
    napalm = "napalm"
    pyats = "pyats"
    scrapli = "scrapli"


class TargetFilters(BaseModel):
    hosts: Union[StrictStr, List[StrictStr]] = Field(
        None, description="Select hostnames to run this task for"
    )

    @staticmethod
    def source_hosts():
        return ["ceos1", "ceos2", "ceos3"]


class DeviceCli(TargetFilters):
    commands: Union[StrictStr, List[StrictStr]] = Field(
        ..., description="CLI commands to send to devices"
    )
    plugin: ConnectionPlugin = Field("netmiko", description="Connection plugin name")

    class PicleConfig:
        subshell = True


class DeviceTools(BaseModel):
    cli: DeviceCli = Field(None, description="Send CLI commands to devices")


class Root(BaseModel):
    devices: DeviceTools = Field(None, description="Device operations")

docs.title: Inline Help
docs.text:
Press ? to show the next valid command field immediately. The current command stays in the input buffer so you can continue editing it after reading the help.

Press ? twice to show the same list with extra details such as defaults and field types.

The key is not inserted into the command buffer. This binding applies only to the main command prompt; ? remains ordinary text in multi-line and chat input.

picle#devices?
 ... available fields under `devices` ...

picle#devices cli commands?
 <'commands' value>    CLI commands to send to devices

picle#devices cli??
 ... the same fields, plus defaults and field types ...

If a field is backed by an enum, help prints the allowed values.

If a model defines source_<field>(), help uses that method to show dynamic choices.

picle#help devices cli plugin
 <'plugin' value>    netmiko, napalm, pyats, scrapli

picle#help devices cli hosts
 <'hosts' value>    ceos1, ceos2, ceos3

If the current model supports subshell entry, help also shows <ENTER>.

picle#help devices cli
 ...
 <ENTER>    Enter command subshell

docs.title: help
docs.text:
help uses the same parser as normal command entry, so it understands nested models, aliases, enum values, and partial matches.

picle#help
 ... top-level commands plus built-in commands like exit, top, pwd, end, cls ...

picle#help devices
 ... fields under `devices` ...

picle#help dev
 ... partial-match help for `devices` ...

docs.title: Tab Completion
docs.text:
Tab completion uses prompt_toolkit for terminal input and delegates candidates to PICLE's existing cmd-style completenames() and completedefault() hooks.

  • The first token completes top-level fields and built-in commands such as exit, top, and help.
  • Nested completion works after you have already entered part of a command path.
  • Enum fields complete from enum values.
  • source_<field> methods feed completion candidates for dynamic values, source_<field> can have choice argument defined to receive partial current value for the field, to alter return options behaviour
  • Multiline fields complete the special load-terminal token.
devices cli <TAB>
  -> suggests fields such as `commands`, `hosts`, and `plugin`

devices cli plugin net<TAB>
  -> completes `netmiko`

devices cli hosts ceos<TAB>
  -> completes values from `source_hosts()`

docs.title: Partial Matches And Suggestions
docs.text:
PICLE distinguishes between incomplete commands and incorrect commands.

picle#dev
Incomplete command, possible completions: devices

If the token does not belong to the current model, PICLE prints an error. When there are close matches, it appends a Did you mean suggestion.

docs.title: Built-in man Commands
docs.text:
App mounts picle.models.MAN automatically under man.

picle#man tree
picle#man tree devices
picle#man json-schema
picle#man json-schema devices.cli

man tree prints a command tree and marks required fields, multiline fields, and dynamic dictionary keys.

man json-schema prints JSON schema for the root model or for a dotted path.

Notes:

  • Dotted paths use field names, aliases, or serialization aliases.
  • man tree requires Rich to render the tree.
  • man json-schema is useful when you want to expose the shell structure as machine-readable data.

docs.title: ConfigModel (configuration shells)
docs.text:
PICLE ships a helper base model for “configuration-mode” shells: picle.models.ConfigModel. It implements a common workflow:

  • Load configuration from YAML (optional dependency: pyyaml)
  • Stage edits into a temporary file (<config_file>.tmp)
  • Review staged changes (show changes) and commit them (commit)
  • Keep rotating backups on commit (.old1, .old2, ...)
  • Roll back by loading a backup into the temp file (rollback <n>) and then committing

docs.title: ConfigModel.PicleConfig keys
docs.text:
ConfigModel reads additional settings from the concrete model’s PicleConfig. These keys are only honored by ConfigModel (the core App ignores them):

Name Meaning config_file Path to the YAML config file (default: configuration.yaml) backup_on_save How many .oldN backups to keep when committing (0 disables backups) commit_hook Optional callable invoked after a successful commit

docs.title: Sample Config Model Shell
docs.text:
Below is example of how to use configuration model to construct interactive shell to manage YAML file content.

"""
Example demonstrating ConfigModel usage in PICLE shells.

This example shows how to create a configuration management system using
ConfigModel to handle YAML configuration files with structured validation.
"""

from enum import Enum
from typing import Optional, Dict
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ConfigDict, StrictStr

from picle.models import ConfigModel, PipeFunctionsModel
from picle.picle import App

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration Structure Models
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------


class SeverityEnum(str, Enum):
    """Logging severity levels."""

    debug = "debug"
    info = "info"
    warning = "warning"
    error = "error"
    critical = "critical"


class TerminalLoggingConfig(BaseModel):
    """Terminal logging configuration."""

    severity: SeverityEnum = Field(
        SeverityEnum.info, description="Logging severity level"
    )
    format: str = Field(None, description="Log message format", alias="format")


class FileLoggingConfig(BaseModel):
    """File logging configuration."""

    enabled: bool = Field(False, description="Enable file logging")
    path: str = Field(None, description="Log file path")
    severity: SeverityEnum = Field(
        SeverityEnum.warning, description="File logging severity level"
    )


class LoggingConfigModel(BaseModel):
    """Main logging configuration."""

    terminal: TerminalLoggingConfig = Field(
        None, description="Terminal logging configuration"
    )
    file: FileLoggingConfig = Field(None, description="File logging configuration")

class WorkerConfigModel(BaseModel):
    timeout: int = Field(None, description="Worker timeout in seconds")
    num_threads: int = Field(None, description="Number of worker threads")
    use_chache: bool = Field(None, description="Whether to use cache for worker results")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration Store with Commands
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------


class MyConfigStore(ConfigModel):
    """
    Configuration store for application settings.

    This model manages YAML configuration files and provides commands
    to view, get, and set configuration values.
    """

    # Configuration structure definition
    logging: LoggingConfigModel = Field(None, description="Logging configuration")
    workers: dict[StrictStr, WorkerConfigModel] = Field(
        None, description="Worker configurations", json_schema_extra={"pkey": "worker_name", "pkey_description": "Name of the worker"}
    )
    class PicleConfig:
        subshell = True
        prompt = "config-shell[cfg]#"
        config_file = "app_config.yaml"  # Default config file path


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Root Shell Model
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------


class RootShell(BaseModel):
    """Root shell with config command."""

    configure_terminal: MyConfigStore = Field(
        None, description="Configuration management commands"
    )

    class PicleConfig:
        pipe = PipeFunctionsModel
        prompt = "config-shell#"


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example Usage
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------


if __name__ == "__main__":
    shell = App(RootShell)
    shell.start()

Above app constructs shell with this commands tree:

config-shell#man tree configure_terminal

R - required field, M - supports multiline input, D - dynamic key

root
└── configure_terminal:    Configuration management commands
    ├── show:    Show commands
    │   ├── configuration:    Show running configuration content
    │   └── changes:    Show uncommitted changes diff between temp and running config
    ├── commit:    Commit pending config changes
    ├── rollback:    Rollback to a backup version
    ├── erase-configuration:    Erase running configuration

config-shell#

And above shell can be used like this:

config-shell[cfg]#workers worker-1 ?

For comprehensive example refer configuration app in test folder of PICLE repository

docs.title: Negating configuration — the no command
docs.text:
Every ConfigModel subclass automatically gains a no command that mirrors the full configuration field tree. It provides the same tab-completion as regular set commands and lets you delete individual keys or entire sub-trees from the staged configuration.

Changes made with no are written to the temp file (same as regular set commands) and only become permanent after commit.

docs.title: Deleting a specific leaf field
docs.text:
Name one or more leaf fields after the path to remove those keys only:

config-shell[cfg]#no workers worker-1 timeout
Configuration negated (uncommitted). Use 'commit' to save or 'show changes' to review.
config-shell[cfg]#show changes
--- app_config.yaml
+++ app_config.yaml.tmp
@@ -1,6 +1,5 @@
 workers:
   worker-1:
     num_threads: 1
-    timeout: 1
     use_cache: true
     worker_name: worker-1
config-shell[cfg]#commit
Configuration committed successfully

Multiple leaf fields can be removed in a single command:

config-shell[cfg]#no workers worker-1 timeout num_threads

docs.title: Deleting an entire sub-tree
docs.text:
Omit leaf fields and the whole node is removed:

config-shell[cfg]#no workers worker-1
Configuration negated (uncommitted). Use 'commit' to save or 'show changes' to review.
config-shell[cfg]#show changes
--- app_config.yaml
+++ app_config.yaml.tmp
@@ -1,6 +1 @@
-workers:
-  worker-1:
-    num_threads: 1
-    timeout: 1
-    use_cache: true
-    worker_name: worker-1
+{}
config-shell[cfg]#commit
Configuration committed successfully

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Pydantic models does not support free-form dictionary keys.

The solution works by creating a temporary, invisible "bridge" when PICLE encounters a Python Dictionary field (Dict[...]).

Here is the simple breakdown.

docs.title: 1. The "Bridge" (VirtualDictModel)
docs.text:
Normally, PICLE looks for exact matches of field names in your Pydantic model. However, a dictionary implies that you get to invent the key name (like name1 or my_entry) at runtime. PICLE cannot know this name in advance.

When PICLE sees a field like mytopkey: Dict[str, MyNestedModel], it creates a special VirtualDictModel. Think of this as a placeholder that says: "I am waiting for one word to serve as the dictionary key."

docs.title: 2. How it flows step-by-step
docs.text:
When you type the command: picle# mytopkey name1 k1 v1

mytopkey: PICLE finds this field in your root model. It sees it is a Dict. It switches to the "Bridge" mode. name1: PICLE expects a key here. It grabs "name1" and says, "Okay, this is the key for our dictionary." Transition: PICLE looks at the dictionary definition (Dict[..., MyNestedModel]). It knows that whatever is under this key must look like MyNestedModel.

k1 v1: PICLE now switches to MyNestedModel and parses k1 v1 just like normal fields.

docs.title: 3. Reconstructing the Data
docs.text: At the end, PICLE takes these three pieces—the field name (mytopkey), the captured key (name1), and the nested data ({'k1': 'v1'})—and stitches them together into the final nested structure:

docs.title: 4. Customizing Help
docs.text: To make the "Bridge" user-friendly, we look at json_schema_extra keys (pkey and pkey_description). PICLE uses these to tell the user: Input name when they ask for help (?). This allows you to mix structured, strict Pydantic models with free-form dictionary keys seamlessly.

docs.title: Field Aliases
docs.text:
PICLE resolves command tokens by canonical field name, alias, or serialization_alias.

This lets you keep Python-friendly field names in code while exposing shell-friendly names such as dashed commands.

docs.title: Example Model
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, StrictStr


class LoginOptions(BaseModel):
    key_path: StrictStr = Field(
        None,
        description="SSH private key",
        alias="key-path",
    )
    user_name: StrictStr = Field(
        ...,
        description="Remote username",
        serialization_alias="user-name",
    )

    @staticmethod
    def run(**kwargs):
        return kwargs

class ConnectCommand(BaseModel):
    transport_mode: StrictStr = Field(
        None,
        description="Connection transport",
        alias="transport-mode",
    )
    login: LoginOptions = Field(None, description="Login parameters")


class Root(BaseModel):
    device_tools: ConnectCommand = Field(
        None,
        description="Device operations",
        alias="device-tools",
    )

docs.title: Command Examples
docs.text:
Top-level and field aliases are accepted anywhere along the path:

picle#device-tools transport-mode ssh
{'transport_mode': 'ssh'}

Nested aliases work the same way:

picle#device-tools login key-path ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 user-name admin
{'key_path': '~/.ssh/id_ed25519', 'user_name': 'admin'}

You can freely mix canonical names and aliases in the same command:

picle#device_tools login key-path ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 user_name admin

docs.title: What Your Code Receives
docs.text:
Aliases affect command resolution, help, completion, and dotted paths used by man json-schema.

The callable still receives canonical field names in kwargs.

That is why the examples above return keys such as transport_mode and user_name, even though the shell input uses dashed names.

docs.title: Fields Presence
docs.text:
presence is useful for boolean-ish flags where you want the value to be set just by mentioning the field.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Root(BaseModel):
    verbose: bool = Field(
        False,
        description="Enable verbose mode",
        json_schema_extra={"presence": True},
    )

    @staticmethod
    def run(**kwargs):
        return kwargs

Example interaction:

picle#verbose
{'verbose': True}

docs.title: Filters And Outputters
docs.text:
This page complements Pipes.

picle.models.PipeFunctionsModel bundles ready-to-use filters and outputters that you can expose with PicleConfig.pipe.

The same outputter callables can also be attached directly to fields or to PicleConfig.outputter.

docs.title: Enabling Built-in Pipe Functions
docs.text:
from typing import Any
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, StrictStr
from picle.models import PipeFunctionsModel


class ShowCommands(BaseModel):
    joke: Any = Field(
        None,
        description="Show a joke",
        json_schema_extra={"function": "show_joke"},
    )
    data: Any = Field(
        None,
        description="Produce structured data",
        json_schema_extra={"function": "produce_data"},
    )
    inventory: Any = Field(
        None,
        description="Produce tabular data",
        json_schema_extra={"function": "produce_inventory"},
    )

    @staticmethod
    def show_joke():
        return """
Why did the network engineer always carry a ladder?

Because he wanted to reach the highest levels of connectivity.

The End.
        """

    @staticmethod
    def produce_data():
        return {
            "some": {"dictionary": {"data": None}},
            "more": {"dictionary": ["data"]},
            "even": {"more": {"dictionary": "data"}},
            "list": [
                {"more": {"dictionary": "data"}},
                {"more": {"dictionary": "data"}},
            ],
        }

    @staticmethod
    def produce_inventory():
        return [
            {"name": "name3", "key1": "key1_value3", "key2": "key2_value3"},
            {"name": "name1", "key1": "key1_value1", "key2": "key2_value1"},
            {"name": "name2", "key1": "key1_value2", "key2": "key2_value2"},
        ]

    class PicleConfig:
        pipe = PipeFunctionsModel


class Notes(BaseModel):
    text: StrictStr = Field(None, description="Markdown or plain text")

    @staticmethod
    def run(**kwargs):
        return kwargs.get("text", "")

    class PicleConfig:
        pipe = PipeFunctionsModel

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
PipeFunctionsModel includes three text filters.

  • include: keep only lines that contain the requested pattern.
  • exclude: drop lines that contain the requested pattern.
  • last: keep only the last N lines.
picle#show joke | include Why
Why did the network engineer always carry a ladder?

picle#show joke | exclude Why
 ... the line containing `Why` is removed ...

picle#show joke | last 1
The End.

Filters are chainable:

picle#show joke | include d | exclude End

docs.title: Structured Outputters
docs.text:
The built-in outputters cover common CLI presentation needs.

  • pprint: Python pretty-print formatting.
  • json: JSON with configurable indentation and sorting.
  • yaml: YAML output when pyyaml is installed.
  • nested: recursive nested formatting, optionally with tabulated lists.
  • kv: flatten nested data into key.path: value lines.
  • table: text tables via tabulate.
  • rich-table: Rich table rendering when Rich is installed.
  • markdown: Rich Markdown rendering when Rich is installed.
  • save: write output to a file.
picle#show data | pprint
{'even': {'more': {'dictionary': 'data'}}, ...}

picle#show data | json
{
    "even": {
        "more": {
            "dictionary": "data"
        }
    },
    ...
}

picle#show data | yaml
even:
  more:
    dictionary: data
...

picle#show data | kv
some.dictionary.data: None
more.dictionary.0: data
even.more.dictionary: data
list.0.more.dictionary: data
list.1.more.dictionary: data

yaml requires pyyaml. table requires tabulate. rich-table and markdown require rich.

docs.title: Table Output
docs.text:
The table outputter is a pipe model with its own fields.

picle#show inventory | table
+----+--------+-------------+-------------+
|    | name   | key1        | key2        |
+====+========+=============+=============+
|  1 | name3  | key1_value3 | key2_value3 |
|  2 | name1  | key1_value1 | key2_value1 |
|  3 | name2  | key1_value2 | key2_value2 |

picle#show inventory | table tablefmt plain
name    key1         key2
 1  name3   key1_value3  key2_value3
 2  name1   key1_value1  key2_value1
 3  name2   key1_value2  key2_value2

picle#show inventory | table sortby name reverse

picle#show inventory | table headers-exclude key2

docs.title: Markdown And Save
docs.text:
Any pipe-enabled command that returns text can be rendered as Markdown or saved to disk.

picle#notes text "# Hello World" | markdown

picle#notes text "hello" | save .\output.txt

save creates parent directories if needed, writes the data to the requested file, and still returns the original result.

docs.title: Input Parsing
docs.text:
PICLE does more than split on spaces.

App.parse_command() has special handling for quoted strings, JSON-like chunks, JSON fields, and scalar conversion.

docs.title: Example Models
docs.text:
from typing import Any, List, Union
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, Json, StrictInt, StrictStr


class RunCommand(BaseModel):
    command: StrictStr = Field(None, description="Command text")

    @staticmethod
    def run(**kwargs):
        return kwargs


class PayloadCommand(BaseModel):
    data: Json[Any] = Field(None, description="JSON payload")
    label: Any = Field(None, description="Label")

    @staticmethod
    def run(**kwargs):
        return kwargs


class LimitsCommand(BaseModel):
    retries: StrictInt = Field(None, description="Retry count")
    name: StrictStr = Field(None, description="Job name")
    threshold: Any = Field(None, description="Threshold")

    @staticmethod
    def run(**kwargs):
        return kwargs


class BatchCommand(BaseModel):
    items: Union[StrictStr, List[StrictStr]] = Field(
        None, description="Collect multiple items"
    )
    tag: StrictStr = Field(None, description="Batch tag")

    @staticmethod
    def run(**kwargs):
        return kwargs


class Root(BaseModel):
    run_command: RunCommand = Field(None, alias="run-command")
    payload: PayloadCommand = Field(None)
    limits: LimitsCommand = Field(None)
    batch: BatchCommand = Field(None)

docs.title: Quoted Values
docs.text:
Single quotes and double quotes let you pass multi-word values as a single field value.

picle#run-command command 'show version | match "Juniper: "'
{'command': 'show version | match "Juniper: "'}

picle#run-command command "hello world"
{'command': 'hello world'}

Double-quoted single-word values work too:

picle#run-command command "hello"
{'command': 'hello'}

docs.title: JSON-like Chunks
docs.text:
If a value starts with { or [, PICLE keeps collecting tokens until it sees a token that ends with the matching closing bracket.

That makes it possible to pass JSON-like text through the shell.

picle#payload data [1, 2, 3] label demo
{'data': '[1, 2, 3]', 'label': 'demo'}

picle#payload data {"person":{"name":"John","age":30}} label demo
{'data': '{"person":{"name":"John","age":30}}', 'label': 'demo'}

docs.title: Json[...] Fields Preserve Raw Input
docs.text:
Json[...] fields are special-cased in the parser.

PICLE keeps the raw text instead of converting values like true, false, or null before Pydantic sees them.

picle#payload data true label demo
{'data': 'true', 'label': 'demo'}

picle#payload data false label demo
{'data': 'false', 'label': 'demo'}

picle#payload data null label demo
{'data': 'null', 'label': 'demo'}

docs.title: Automatic Scalar Conversion
docs.text:
For non-str fields, PICLE tries a lightweight conversion pass before validation.

  • True, False, and None become Python values.
  • Digit-only values become int.
  • Values containing . are tried as float.
picle#limits retries 3 threshold 3.14 name nightly
{'retries': 3, 'threshold': 3.14, 'name': 'nightly'}

String fields keep their string representation:

picle#limits name 123
{'name': '123'}

docs.title: Repeating A Field
docs.text:
If your field accepts list-like input, you can repeat the field name to collect multiple values.

picle#batch items val1 items val2 items val3 tag nightly
{'items': ['val1', 'val2', 'val3'], 'tag': 'nightly'}

Use this pattern when you want explicit, readable shell grammar for list input.

docs.title: Mounting/removing models at runtime
docs.text:
App can add/remove models to the root tree:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, StrictStr
from picle import App


class Mounted(BaseModel):
    param: StrictStr = Field(None, description="Param string")

    @staticmethod
    def run(**kwargs):
        return kwargs


class Root(BaseModel):
    command: StrictStr = Field(None, description="Some command")


shell = App(Root)
shell.model_mount(Mounted, ["another_command"])
shell.model_remove(["another_command"])

Notes:

  • path may be a list of segments or a single string.
  • model_mount can only mount under an existing path, except for the final segment (which is created).
  • Mounted fields are added to the root model’s model_fields and participate in completion/help.

docs.title: Multi-line Input
docs.text:
If a field enables multi-line input, the user can type the literal value load-terminal to start collection.

PICLE reads lines until EOF and uses the collected text (joined by \n) as the field value. At an empty input prompt, press Ctrl+D to finish collection on Linux, macOS, or Windows.

from typing import Any
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, StrictStr


class NotesCommand(BaseModel):
    body: StrictStr = Field(
        None,
        description="Multi-line note body",
        json_schema_extra={"multiline": True},
    )
    title: Any = Field(None, description="Note title")

    @staticmethod
    def run(**kwargs):
        return kwargs


class Root(BaseModel):
    notes: NotesCommand = Field(
        None,
        description="Create a note",
    )

Help shows the load-terminal option when appropriate:

picle#notes body ?
 <'body' value>    Multi-line note body
 load-terminal     Collect value using multi line input mode

Invoking multi-line collection:

picle#notes body load-terminal
Enter lines and hit Ctrl+D to finish multi line input
line 1
line 2
<Ctrl+D>

The collected value is then validated and passed to your callable as a single string containing embedded newlines.

docs.title: Pipes
docs.text:
If PicleConfig class pipe is set, the | token becomes valid and starts a new “segment”. The next segment is parsed using the pipe model. pipe can be:

"self"                  re-use the current model as the pipe model
"some.module.Model"     import a model by string
SomeModelClass          use a model class directly

Example - enable pipe functions:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from picle.models import PipeFunctionsModel, Outputters


class ShellModel(BaseModel):
    class PicleConfig:
        prompt = "picle#"
        intro = "PICLE Sample app"
        pipe = PipeFunctionsModel

!!! note processors run on the first command segment only (before any | segments). They do not apply to subsequent pipe segments. If you want to post-process the output of a pipe segment, use an outputter or a pipe function in that segment.

docs.title: Processors
docs.text:
Processors are just functions that transform results. They run in order.

from typing import Any
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from picle.models import Outputters


class ModelShow(BaseModel):
    data_pprint: Any = Field(
        None,
        description="Show structured data using pprint",
        json_schema_extra={
            "function": "produce_structured_data",
            "processors": [Outputters.outputter_pprint],
        },
    )

    @staticmethod
    def produce_structured_data():
        return {"some": {"nested": {"data": None}}}

If you also set PicleConfig.processors, they run for the first segment after field-level processors.

docs.title: Result-specific Outputters
docs.text:
Sometimes a single model-level outputter is not enough. If you need to choose an outputter based on runtime data, return a tuple from run():

(result, outputter)
(result, outputter, outputter_kwargs)

This overrides model and field outputters for that specific execution.

docs.title: Shell Commands
docs.text:
PICLE provides a built-in shell command to execute operating system shell commands directly from the interactive prompt.

This command works on Windows and Linux.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Use the command as:

shell <command>

Examples:

picle#shell echo hello
hello

picle#shell python --version
Python 3.x.x

The command is global, so it can be used from the top prompt and from subshells.

docs.title: Platform Behavior
docs.text:
shell executes commands via Python subprocess.run(...) with shell=True.

  • On Windows, commands run through the system shell (for example cmd.exe).
  • On Linux, commands run through the default shell (for example /bin/sh).

This means you can use native shell commands for each platform.

# Windows
picle#shell dir

# Linux
picle#shell ls -la

docs.title: Output And Errors
docs.text:
PICLE captures and prints both standard output and error output:

  • stdout is printed as regular command output.
  • stderr is printed using error output formatting.
  • If a command exits with a non-zero code and produced no stderr, PICLE prints the exit code.

If no command is provided, PICLE returns:

shell command is required

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
Use built-in help to see command documentation:

picle#help shell

docs.title: Security Note
docs.text: shell runs commands on the host operating system, so avoid passing untrusted input directly into it.

docs.title: Subshells And Navigation
docs.text:
If a model sets PicleConfig.subshell = True, entering that model without arguments pushes it onto the shell stack and changes the prompt.

This makes large command trees easier to use because you can navigate once and then run shorter commands inside the subshell.

docs.title: Example Model
docs.text:
from enum import Enum
from typing import List, Union
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, StrictBool, StrictStr


class ConnectionPlugin(str, Enum):
    netmiko = "netmiko"
    napalm = "napalm"


class DeviceCli(BaseModel):
    commands: Union[StrictStr, List[StrictStr]] = Field(
        ..., description="CLI commands to send to devices"
    )
    plugin: ConnectionPlugin = Field("netmiko", description="Connection plugin name")
    add_details: StrictBool = Field(
        None,
        description="Show detailed output",
        json_schema_extra={"presence": True},
    )

    @staticmethod
    def run(**kwargs):
        return f"Called device cli, kwargs: {kwargs}"

    class PicleConfig:
        subshell = True
        prompt = "devices[cli]#"


class DeviceTools(BaseModel):
    cli: DeviceCli = Field(None, description="Send CLI commands to devices")

    class PicleConfig:
        subshell = True
        prompt = "devices#"


class Root(BaseModel):
    target: StrictStr = Field("lab", description="Device group")
    platform: StrictStr = Field("eos", description="Device platform")
    devices: DeviceTools = Field(None, description="Device commands")

docs.title: Entering A Subshell
docs.text:
picle#devices cli
devices[cli]#commands "show clock" add_details
Called device cli, kwargs: {
    'target': 'lab',
    'platform': 'eos',
    'plugin': 'netmiko',
    'commands': 'show clock',
    'add_details': True
}

You can also enter intermediate shells:

picle#devices
devices#

docs.title: Defaults Follow You
docs.text:
When you enter a subshell, PICLE keeps non-None defaults from the current shell path in shell_defaults.

In the example above, the command inside devices[cli]# inherits:

  • target = "lab"
  • platform = "eos"
  • plugin = "netmiko"

That is why commands "show clock" is enough once you are already inside the CLI subshell.

Leaving the subshell with exit or resetting with top clears the inherited defaults appropriately.

docs.title: Built-in Navigation Commands
docs.text:
PICLE exposes several global shell commands:

  • exit: leave the current subshell, or terminate if already at the top level.
  • top: return to the root shell and reset the shell stack.
  • end: terminate the application immediately.
  • pwd: print the current shell path.
  • cls: clear the terminal screen.
  • history: print command history.
devices[cli]#pwd
Root->DeviceTools->DeviceCli

devices[cli]#exit
devices#

devices#top
picle#

Notes:

  • Interactive history uses the same persistent prompt_toolkit session on Linux, macOS, and Windows.
  • PicleConfig.history_file selects the history file, and history_length limits the number of entries written when the shell exits.
  • History output skips meta commands such as help, history, exit, and commands ending in ?.
